message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Budget Justification, Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries (Westmoor)

## What the bid asks for

Library Services is asking for £174,000 a year to extend five branch libraries by ten hours a week each: Tuesday and Thursday evenings until 8 pm, plus Sunday 11 am to 3 pm. The case rests on a pilot at Ashgrove that used exactly this pattern. That pilot showed strong Sunday use, a fully booked evening job club, and new memberships up about two-thirds. The bid also argues that the extra hours would cost about £2 per visit, against a borough average of £3.40.

Testing the exact pattern before asking for funding is the right approach, and the Sunday results and the job club are good evidence. But several of the bid's key statements don't match its own tables:
- The cost total is wrong.
- Evening use was well below daytime use, not close to it.
- The pilot lasted six months, not twelve.
- The value-for-money comparison assumes Ashgrove's usage at all five branches and compares marginal cost with full cost.

## 1. The costs add up to £164,000, not £174,000

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Staffing (5,000 hours × £24.80) | £124,000 |
| Utilities and caretaking (5 × £6,500) | £32,500 |
| Kiosk maintenance | £7,500 |
| **Sum** | **£164,000** |

The total in the table, and the amount requested, is **£10,000 higher** than the items add up to. Either a cost line is missing or the total is wrong. This needs correcting before the bid goes to Members.

There are also some issues within the lines:
- **Holiday pay isn't included.** "50 weeks a year" covers bank holiday closures, but not staff annual leave. Additional contracted hours earn holiday entitlement of about 12% on top, which must be paid or covered. On that basis the staffing line is likely understated.
- **The Sunday enhancement may be applied to every hour.** The text says the £24.80 rate includes a Sunday enhancement. If that rate is used for all 5,000 hours, the evening hours are overcosted. Please show the evening and Sunday rates separately.
- **Utilities are probably overstated, which is a cautious error.** The pilot ran from October to March, when heating and lighting costs peak. Scaling those months up to a full year likely overstates the cost.
- **The kiosk maintenance line needs explaining.** The extra hours are fully staffed, so it isn't clear why kiosk maintenance is part of this bid.

## 2. Evening use was well below daytime use

Section 3 and the Conclusion both say evening visits "averaged close to the weekday daytime level." Table 1 shows otherwise:

| Slot | Visits per hour |
|---|---|
| Weekday daytime | 46–58 |
| **Tuesday/Thursday evening (new)** | **21** |
| Sunday (new) | 52 |

Evening use ran at **about 40% of weekday daytime use**. Sunday use was strong. Evening use was modest, apart from the job club. The claim of "strong latent demand for evening opening… across all five branches" doesn't follow from these figures.

## 3. The pilot ran for six months, not twelve

Table 1 covers October 2025 to March 2026, which is six months. The Conclusion calls it a "twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." Six months is still useful evidence, but the description should match it. A winter-only pilot may also understate evening use in lighter months, which is worth saying.

## 4. The value-for-money figure is too favourable

The 84,000 visits figure assumes **every branch matches Ashgrove**. Per branch per week, that is 6 evening hours × 21 plus 4 Sunday hours × 52, or 334 visits. Over 50 weeks and five branches, that comes to about 83,500 visits.

But Section 7 says Ashgrove is the busiest branch and the other four may see less demand. The estimate should use each branch's own usage, for example by scaling Ashgrove's figures by each branch's current visits relative to Ashgrove.

Two further problems:
- **Not every visit is new.** Some people who now come on Sunday would otherwise have come on Saturday or a weekday. The bid needs to show whether visits in existing hours at Ashgrove fell during the pilot.
- **The comparison isn't like for like.** £2 per visit is the *extra* cost of opening additional hours, in a building that already has its stock, staff and premises costs paid for. £3.40 is the borough's *full* cost per visit, including all of those. The marginal figure will always look cheaper. A fairer test compares cost per *additional* visit with what other ways of reaching working-age residents would cost.

## 5. The self-service option is cheaper over time

The author's summary says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The paper itself doesn't claim that, and its own figures suggest the reverse:
- **Annual saving:** cutting staffing by about two-thirds saves roughly £83,000 a year.
- **One-off cost:** building works are about £300,000 (£60,000 × 5), usually funded as capital rather than from the annual budget.
- **Breakeven:** the saving pays back the building works in roughly 3.6 years.

The stronger argument for staffed opening is the one the paper does make. Self-service can't run the job club or family activities. Given how differently the two slots performed, a **mixed approach** is worth costing: staffed Sundays, plus the job club evening, with lighter or self-service cover on the other evening.

## 6. Smaller points

- **The membership increase can't be credited solely to the new hours.** It rose 65% (1,140 against 690), but the paper should say whether there were any membership campaigns, school drives or other changes over the same period.
- **Recruitment.** Relying on existing part-time staff is plausible for one branch. Five branches need about 100 extra staff hours a week, so it's worth checking that enough staff want the extra hours.
- **The six-month review should have consequences.** Say what happens if a branch falls below a set usage threshold, for example dropping its evening hours.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the total to £164,000 or identify the missing £10,000 line. Add holiday pay, and show evening and Sunday rates separately.
2. Correct the evening-use claim. Evenings ran at about 40% of daytime use, and Sundays matched daytime.
3. Describe the pilot as six months, in winter.
4. Estimate visits branch by branch, allow for visits shifting from other hours, and drop or reframe the comparison with £3.40.
5. Present self-service as cheaper over time but unable to support activities, and cost a mixed option.
6. Consider phasing: Sunday opening at all five branches, and evening opening where there is a job club or other evidence of demand.

The Sunday case is strong and the job club is a real success. With the corrections above, a revised bid, possibly smaller and focused on Sundays, would be easier for Members to approve and to defend.
